reason: A leaf apex or tip can be filiform (thread-like). The examples are correct.
Lobes are commonly semicircular. The examples are correct.
Flower bracts can be hairy or glabrous. The examples (glabrescent, puberulent) are correct hair-cover states.
The examples count veins or nerves of a leaf (few lateral veins), not vascular bundles. The part is a wrong reading. A rule should map 'veins few' to the leaf or vein part.
A rhizome or rootstock crown can be woolly (lanate). The examples are correct.
A pyrene (the stone of a drupe) can be oblong. The examples are correct.
Anther thecae are measured in width and length. The examples are correct.
A moss operculum can be plicate. The examples are correct.
A costa or fern rachis can be terete (round in section). The examples are correct.
An ochrea (stipular sheath) can have a truncate apex or mouth. The examples are correct.

Perforate fits a leaf blade with holes, as in Monstera. Several examples describe pores in hyaline cells (Sphagnum) or the midrib. A rule would need to tell leaf perforations from cell pores, which belong to the cell part.
The examples describe a gland as terete, so the shape is sensible. The bearer here is the tissue portion, not the gland organ. The pair is only right if the rule maps 'gland' to this PO class.
Cymes can be opposite (arrangement on the axis). The examples are correct.
Inflorescence axes and rachises can be hairy or glabrous. The examples are correct.
An androphore can be short. The examples are correct.
Reticulate ornamentation is a pattern and fits. 'Paired' teeth or cilia is an arrangement, not a pattern. A rule would need to separate surface patterns from arrangement words.
A thallus is measured in length and width. The examples are correct.

'Erect or spreading' and 'inserted at the mouth' are position or orientation and fit. 'Striate horizontally' is surface ornamentation. A rule would need to separate position or orientation words from ornamentation.
Alar cell regions can be small. The examples are correct.
Alar cells are described as well differentiated in mosses. The example is correct.
Spore shape is a valid attribute. The examples (oval) are correct.
A moss calyptra can be inflated around the capsule. The example is correct.
A capsule can be bilaterally symmetric. The examples are correct.
The examples are plain measurements ('1–2 cm long'), which are length values, not 'increased length'. The pair comes from a wrong reading of the quality. A rule should map measurements to length.
The examples are about pores in superficial cortical cells. That is a cell trait, not a stem trait, so the part is wrong. A rule should send these to the cell part.
Sphagnum hyaline cells are fibrillose (with fibril thickenings). The examples are correct.
A primary vein can be hairy or glabrous. The examples are correct.
A rachis can be grooved (canaliculate). The examples are correct.
A rachis can bear glands below the pinna pairs, so it is glandular. The examples are correct.
Pods or their parts can be reflexed. The examples are correct, though the bearer may be a part of the pod.
The examples describe ridges, a lateral rim and an upper part, which are not the androgynophore. The part is a wrong reading.
Style branches can be hairy, including with collecting hairs. The examples are correct.
The examples ('le haut', 'base', 'partie inférieure canaliculée') point to a petiole or stalk rather than an orchid labellum. The part is a wrong reading.
A connective appendage can be ovate. The examples are correct.
Ray flowers are ligulate (strap-shaped). The examples are correct.
Lateral ovules is a placement and is meaningful. 'Lateral to' is a relation that needs a reference part. A rule would need to say what the ovules are lateral to, or map this to a placement term.
Bracts can be lepidote (scaly). The examples are correct.
Leaflet venation can be brochidodromous. The examples are correct.
'Stems annual to perennial' fits a stem. 'Annual or biennial' with stems is often really the whole plant's life span. A rule would need to tell stem-specific wording from plant habit.
Root nodules can vary in shape (linear, elliptic, dot-like). The examples are correct.
The examples (abortive, margined, jointed to the rachis) are unrelated features, not a quality of structure. This is a wrong reading, and the examples also describe other parts.
A petiolule can be winged. The examples are correct.
Mericarps can be spiny. The negated examples ('without spines') need the absence rule.
A capsule can have a truncate apex or base. The examples are correct.
Pinnae can overlap. The 'overlapping rachis' example is odd, but the pair is sound.
Capsules can be sessile or stipitate. The examples are correct.
A rosette has a height or diameter. The examples are correct, though the dm size example is a mixed measurement.
Phyllaries can be spotted. The examples are correct.
Lobes can be flat (plane). The examples are correct.
A leaf blade outline can be irregular. The examples are correct, though areolation is a different feature.
A fruit can be solid, as opposed to hollow. The examples are correct.
A perianth can be striped or banded. The examples are correct.

The examples are about whether stereids are present in a costa or leaf section. The bearer should be the costa or leaf, and the stereid is the part that is present. A rule is needed for presence of a part on a stereid-bearing organ.
Spikes can be elongate. The examples are correct.
A perigynium surface can be dull or shiny. The example is correct.
A perigynium beak has a colour. The examples are correct.
Sepals or their parts can be colourless. The examples include hairs and lobes, so the bearer may be a sepal part.
Pappus scales can be linear. The examples are correct.
A bract can be glutinous. The examples describe a glutinous ridge on the bract face, so the bearer is the ridge. A rule would need to tell bract-wide stickiness from a feature on the bract.
The examples ('lateral veins weak') describe veins, not the leaf. The part is wrong. A rule should assign them to the vein.
